questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I wanted to go somewhere, where i felt i could speak to locals and which had a more international environment. There weren't that many different opportunities for physics students in the EU, which had many bachelor courses in english, and was a city i could see myself living in. 
I had heard great stuff about Amsterdam, and when i saw they had a decent selection of courses, i felt that i was a good choice.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: UvA's website was actually pretty good. A lot of useful information, and most importantly the course catalogue on Studiegids was very clear and easy to navigate.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had an introduction day for science exchange students, which was good. It was just a welcome and some basic information, as well as an opportunity to get to know other exchange students and ask the staff questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Housing is definitely the biggest problem with going to Amsterdam (or the Netherlands in general). There is a crazy housing crisis - and i mean really bad... The university did warn about this on their website and they are not joking.

I signed up for the housing lottery organized by the university and simply got lucky, that i got a sport. Once they have confirmed you got a spot, turn on notifications on your email. When the different housing offers are being released, it's all about being quick. When booking my room, i could see the rooms disappearing from the list just minutes after the link was sent out. I got Lieven De Key as my housing provider, and if you get them CHOOSE PRINSENGRACHT. You really can't live a nicer place location-wise, and it's also just nice rooms and good social life. 

You need to have a back-up plan in case you don't get a spot, or be okay with cancelling your exchange if you don't manage to get housing. Also, i think it really made a difference for my social life on exchange that i was in student housing with other exchange students, instead of having rented something from a private person.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It's easy to get around the city because bikes :) Also public transport is very good. So i would prioritize living in a nice area over being close to campus. Especially because Science Park isn't the most charming place.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: ^I was sooo happy about my housing, but the general housing situation is not great - therefore the 3/5

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I don't really remember in detail. 
The registration was pretty easy. I think the university sent emails, whenever you had to do something and there was a site, where you could upload stuff etc. 
The only thing that was confusing was, that for some minors the registration was through a Google Survey or something, and then later on you would be accepted for the courses. 

So the normal registration was completely fine, but for some minors it was a bit messy.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I didnt really struggle that much, so i didnt reach out for help. But i think you could just write the international student office an email.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Got all i wanted, apart from one course. But i got my second priority, so it wasn't a big problem.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Read your emails :)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I would say on average the level is pretty similar to UCPH. But just like UCPH the difference in the level and workload of the courses can be very different. 

The biggest difference for me was that all exams i had where either completely without notes or only with very few. So you have to adjust to that, because i was used to being allowed notes, book, computer etc. at most of my previous exams.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Most courses were pretty similar with lectures and then problem classes. As mentioned, one of the biggest differences for me were the exams. 
Also i feel like i did more group work than at UCPH, though not all was mandatory. 

If you don't like the block structure, you should rethink studing at UvA. Instead of 2 blocks it's 3. 
Block 1 and 2 are 7 weeks each with 2 courses, and block 3 is only 4 (!) weeks with one course. 
The biggest difference compared to UCPH is that there is no week for preparation for the exams and also no free week after exams. 
So essentially you go directly from block 1 to block 2, then you have Christmas break without worrying about exams, which is nice. And then block 3 is in January. Because it's so short, its normally a more project oriented course.
Also, i think there are more assignments, but i feel like they try to help you keep up with the course. Midterms are used much more than at UCPH, i had midterms in 2 courses, and it seemed like most other people i knew also had at least one midterm in both block 1 and 2

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Advanced Quantum Physics
History and Philosophy of Science
Introduction Quantum Computing
Introduction Computational Science
Workshop Physics and Astronomy

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Advanced Quantum Physics was pretty hard for me, but it was the first time that the lecturer had that course, which might explain why he set the bar a bit too high. The lectures were a bit boring, i would say it was a very standard course. 

History and Philosophy of Science was surprisingly good. Kind of a humanities course, but the focus is on science. There is an essay each week, which i wasnt a big fan of. I feel like the course is pretty easy to pass, but not that easy to get a really good grade in. The exam was totally fine. 
So you need to be alright with some philosophy yap and writing essays, but then you get some fun facts about Einstein on the way. 

Introduction Quantum Computing was the best course i had. The lecturer was soooo structured it was amazing. He recorded every lecture and put up the notes. It wasnt too hard, but i still feel like i learned a lot. Good mix of classic problem classes and coding exercises. Would definitely recommend!

Introduction Computational Science was pretty nice as well. The material isnt that hard to understand, but the assignments take a while to do. But if you are all right with coding a lot, i would recommend it. And it was nice to have an interdisciplinary course. I think it is most useful for bio-physics, but it was very good coding practice. 

Workshop Physics and Astronomy is a bit of a hit or miss. There wasnt really any other physics course in block 3. It is like a preparation course for the bachelor thesis, so if you want to take the course, make sure to write the course coordinator already sometime in september, so you are sure to get all the information about the course. 
You choose a workshop, theres astro, hospital physics etc. And then you make some kind of mini project/presentation/report. I did API workshop, which was astrophysics. It was sooo chill and that was great because then i could enjoy my last month in the city ;)
Other workshops seemed like much more work, especially the Nikhef one.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing unexpected really. I choose to rent a bike with Swapfiets, which was totally worth it. Around 20 euros a month, but if anything breaks, the repair is free. And you dont have to worry about getting rid of it once the exchange is over.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries and cafés were less expensive than i expected. I thought it would be the same as in Denmark, because the housing prices seemed to be very similar. But i would say it was more somewhere in between Germany and Denmark depending on which supermarket you went to. 

Public transport was as expensive as Denmark though, but just bike everywhere :) Memberships for sports other than a normal gym membership were also pretty expensive like in Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
A decent amount, but i didnt do that much myself. 
Science Park has really nice sports facilities: big gym, climbing wall, saunas, squash, tennis etc. So there were lots of opportunities to do something. 
For social activities i was just lucky, because i kind of had that with my student housing.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Do some kind of sport, because many of the facilities are on the campuses so it's a good way to meet other students. And if you are not staying at some kind of student housing, befriend someone who does and go to their parties and stuff.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
It's a small country, so do some daytrips. Go see Utrecht, Leiden, Delft, Haarlem, Haag, Maastricht, all very cute cities. 
For longer trips Paris, London and many cities in Germany are just a train ride away. Belgium as well. 

But there is also a lot to do in Amsterdam!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, it's similar to Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just talk to people and ask them questions, because as an exchange student, you will definitely have some. I found most locals to be very friendly and open.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None really.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Biking, but i am kind of used to that. Everything was very efficient and digitalized, which was nice.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Enjoy the city, it's beautiful and fun. Especially walk along the canals and hang out in Jordaan and De Pijp. Nightlife is good as well. Try stroopwafels (from the food markets), indonesian food and other Amsterdam specialties ;)
2. Make sure you are all right with the block structure at uni, but also, remember that everything is pass/fail, so allow yourself to experience the city and country instead studying all of the time. 
3. Hope that you win in the housing lottery, and have a plan B if you don't or consider not going. As mentioned, the housing situation is crazy.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The people i met (most were from my housing), and getting to enjoy such an amazing city with them.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Trying to balance studying and wanting to explore

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
